BXL-2425-00029-v4.headline: Stop taxing university student housing: exempt non-profit student rooms owned by universities and colleges from the regional property tax from 2026, after the tax office started billing them.
BXL-2425-00029-v4.proposed_by: Celia Groothedde (Groen), Martin Casier (PS) and co-signers across several groups
BXL-2425-00029-v4.source_brief:
A 2017 rewrite of the Income Tax Code left it unclear whether student rooms (kots) owned by Brussels universities and colleges still escaped the regional property tax. The tax office read the ambiguity as meaning the exemption was gone and began billing; this text settles the question by writing the exemption back in, but only from 2026 onward.

- **Who it touches:** students renting public, below-market rooms from institutions like the ULB and VUB, where any tax landing on the building eventually shows up in the rent.
- **The money already in dispute:** an administration note put the 2018-2024 billing for the communes concerned at roughly 1.7 million euros, much of it already contested in administrative and court proceedings.
- **The deliberate gap:** the fix is not retroactive, so the 2017-2025 period is left for the institutions, the Region and the courts to settle separately.
- **The rub:** whether a tax break for university-owned housing is a sensible way to keep student rents down, or a carve-out that quietly costs communes revenue they were starting to collect.
deep_facts: The text is a proposition d'ordonnance modifying the Code des impots sur les revenus 1992; the operative provision concerns article 253, paragraph 4, inserted by a 2017 ordinance that entered into force on 1 January 2018 (CRI, 27 Jun 2025).

The stated problem: the 2017 wording created doubt over whether the property-tax (precompte immobilier) exemption for student housing owned by universities and hautes ecoles survived; such housing had previously been exempt without contestation, but Bruxelles Fiscalite read the new text as having removed the exemption and enrolled the buildings for the tax (CRI, 27 Jun 2025).

Per an administration note circulated about two hours before the committee meeting, the enrolment for 2018-2024 across the communes concerned was of the order of 1.7 million euros [estime]; of that, 700.000 euros are the subject of pending administrative reclamations and more than 800.000 euros the subject of pending judicial recours, with the 800.000 figure not yet including the 2024 enrolment (CRI, 27 Jun 2025).

The ordinance is prospective only: it is stated to take effect on 1 January 2026 and to change nothing for the past, deliberately, to avoid adding legal uncertainty while institutions' court cases against the Region proceed; for this reason proposers considered an avis of the Conseil d'Etat unnecessary (CRI, 27 Jun 2025).

Context figures cited in debate: average kot rent of about 680 euros per month, rising roughly 5% per year, described as the highest in Belgium; more than 100.000 students in Brussels; a year of higher education in the Federation Wallonie-Bruxelles said to cost between 12.000 and 15.000 euros, with housing the largest share (CRI, 27 Jun 2025).

Mechanism cited: where the tax is billed, paid and immediately contested then frozen, the Region currently must later repay the sums with interest of 4% on the total annual amount; proposers argue the exemption is therefore cheaper for Region and communes than the status quo (CRI, 27 Jun 2025).

A speaker reported that one institution must cover about 1 million euros a year on student housing, of which 200.000 euros goes to loan repayments and 800.000 euros to advancing and paying rent students cannot themselves pay; another reported the VUB had to raise its own kot rents by 10% after the fiscal change (CRI, 27 Jun 2025).

One original co-signer (Olivier Willocx, MR) announced he was withdrawing his name from the proposal "for reasons you are aware of" while still supporting the text's fiscal-clarity principle (CRI, 27 Jun 2025).

Proposers note that in 2018 the Mesa is not at issue here; rather, they cite a 2007 Flemish circular treating such student housing as an essential education service warranting property-tax exemption, and argue other Regions exempt this housing, so taxing it in Brussels would create unfair competition pushing students toward Ghent, Antwerp or Leuven (CRI, 27 Jun 2025).
BXL-2425-00029-v4.deep_lectura:
**Analyst read** *(inference — not stated verbatim in the record)*

- The non-retroactivity is the crux of the bargain: it lets the assembly affirm the exemption going forward without conceding the 2018-2025 bills, which would directly hit some communes' budgets and pre-empt live litigation — so the text buys consensus precisely by not touching the contested money.
- Pitching it as revenue-neutral or even cheaper (the 4% repayment-with-interest argument) is what lets fiscally cautious groups vote yes without owning a 'tax cut for universities' framing.
- The competition-with-Flanders argument reframes a social-housing measure as a defensive economic one, broadening the coalition beyond left groups to include market-minded members.
- Skipping the Conseil d'Etat avis trims weeks off the timetable but leaves the prospective-only design as the main shield against a later legality challenge.
BXL-2425-00029-v4.raw_fr: La proposition d'ordonnance modifie le Code des impots sur les revenus 1992 afin de clarifier que les logements etudiants proposes sans but lucratif par les universites et hautes ecoles sont exoneres du precompte immobilier. L'article 253, paragraphe 4, insere par une ordonnance de 2017 entree en vigueur le 1er janvier 2018, avait cree un doute sur le maintien de cette exoneration. Le texte n'est pas retroactif et entrerait en vigueur le 1er janvier 2026.

BXL-2425-00029-v7.headline: Let the public Guarantee Fund stand behind more bank loans for small Brussels firms and the self-employed — raising its ceiling from 62 to 90 million euros, at no extra cost to the regional budget.
BXL-2425-00029-v7.proposed_by: Farida Tahar, Zakia Khattabi (Ecolo) and co-signers
BXL-2425-00029-v7.source_brief:
The Brussels Guarantee Fund, created in 1999, stands surety so that small firms and self-employed people who would otherwise be refused can still get a bank loan. Its ceiling has not moved in 25 years and is close to being hit; this text lifts it from 62 to 90 million euros so the Fund can keep backing new credit.

- **Who it touches:** entrepreneurs, shopkeepers and self-employed people who lack family backing or an easy bank yes, and rely on the public guarantee to get financed.
- **The cost claim:** backers stress the rise needs no extra subsidy — the Fund is built to run at balance, funded by premiums from banks and beneficiary firms, and only pays out on default or bankruptcy (about 13-15% of amounts granted).
- **Why now:** the ceiling was about 90% used in March and projected to hit 100% in September, which is why the text was brought urgently.
- **The rub:** whether expanding public exposure backing private loans is smart leverage for the local economy at near-zero budget cost, or a near-100-million-euro commitment waved through with thin oversight of how the Fund actually performs.
deep_facts: The text (proposition d'ordonnance, dossier A-116) raises the Guarantee Fund's intervention ceiling (plafond d'intervention / d'engagement) from 62 million euros to 90 million euros; this is the object of article 2 (CRI, 27 Jun 2025).

The Fonds bruxellois de garantie was created in 1999 to support entrepreneurship by facilitating SME and self-employed access to professional credit; the ceiling has not changed since 1999, cited as nearly 62 million euros (CRI, 27 Jun 2025).

Budget framing: the Fund is designed to run at equilibrium without increased regional subsidy; the subsidy is fixed at 1.125.000 euros; backers state no fund increase is needed for the ceiling rise, current budget plus rising premiums from banks and beneficiary firms being sufficient; over the last two years the Fund reportedly partly repaid its subsidy to the Region (CRI, 27 Jun 2025).
The guarantee intervenes only in last resort, on default or bankruptcy, concerning 13 to 15% of amounts granted (CRI, 27 Jun 2025).

Activity figures cited: in 2024 the Fund activated 42 million euros of credit benefiting 153 firms; over seven years, 4.164 jobs generated, 90 million euros granted and 621 firms supported (CRI, 27 Jun 2025).
Urgency rationale: the existing ceiling was about 90% reached in March and projected to reach 100% in September, prompting urgent submission (CRI, 27 Jun 2025).

The text allows raising the ceiling further by up to four additional tranches of 12,5 million euros each; under the version proposed, activating a tranche requires notification to (not prior approval of) the Parliament (CRI, 27 Jun 2025).

An oversight clause (article 19.1) added in committee and obligations under article 23 of the 1999 ordinance provide for parliamentary reporting; an arrete of 25 May 2022 already requires the Fund's board to inform the competent minister when a 75% threshold is exceeded (CRI, 27 Jun 2025).

A safeguard cited: if the average default rate across active engagements exceeds 20% in a budget year, the Government suspends any new tranche activation and submits a thorough evaluation to the Parliament with a view to possible revision of the engagement ceiling (CRI, 27 Jun 2025).

A contested point: one group stated the Parliament has received no annual report, balance sheet or accounts directly from the Guarantee Fund since 2018 (the last report dating from 2018, on amounts cited as 61 million euros), and that the Fund's administrators do not appear in the UBO register; proposers replied that activity reports are published on the finance&invest.brussels website (e.g. pages 38-39 of the 2023 report) and that a Fund official answered all questions in committee (CRI, 27 Jun 2025).
An initial version reportedly proposed a higher ceiling (figures of 100 million and even 125 million euros were referenced in debate) before being brought down to 90 million euros (CRI, 27 Jun 2025).
BXL-2425-00029-v7.deep_lectura:
**Analyst read** *(inference — not stated verbatim in the record)*

- The decisive selling point is 'budget-neutral': in a tight fiscal context, a measure that expands support without new spending is the rare lever almost every group can back, which is why the debate is about oversight, not about the ceiling itself.
- The 90-million figure reads as a negotiated landing point — down from 100-125 million — calibrated to projections plus a safety margin, trading maximal headroom for broad buy-in.
- The tranche mechanism (four x 12,5 million, notification not approval) hands the government future capacity to keep raising exposure without returning for a full vote, which is exactly the slippage the transparency fight is really about.
- The 'no report since 2018 / no UBO entry' charge, if accurate, matters beyond this vote: it questions whether the existing controls the majority leans on to call new oversight redundant are actually being honoured.
BXL-2425-00029-v7.raw_fr: La proposition d'ordonnance vise a accroitre le plafond d'intervention du Fonds bruxellois de garantie, qui passerait de 62 millions d'euros a 90 millions d'euros (objet de l'article 2). Cree en 1999, le Fonds facilite l'acces au credit professionnel pour les PME et les independants et est concu pour fonctionner a l'equilibre, sans accroissement des subsides regionaux. Rien qu'en 2024, le fonds a permis d'activer 42 millions d'euros de credits au benefice de 153 entreprises.

BXL-2425-00029-v5.headline: Rewrite the transparency rules of the public fund that guarantees small-business loans: its accounts and board report must reach the government and Parliament by 30 June every year — but Parliament's prior say over expanding the Fund becomes a simple notification.
BXL-2425-00029-v5.source_brief:
Bolted onto the ordinance raising the Guarantee Fund's ceiling is this rival amendment over how the Fund reports to Parliament. It would scrap and rewrite the whole reporting article (art. 23), folding in useful bits of a separately added clause, and set a clear annual deadline — but, critics note, it swaps Parliament's prior say on extra credit tranches for a mere notification.

- **What it changes:** the board would have to send the balance sheet, results and audit report directly to the government and Parliament by 30 June each year — later than the existing 30 April deadline, which the mover argues is impossible to meet since accounts are approved in May.
- **The oversight catch:** the mover frames it as fixing a drafting muddle and modernising one clean clause; opponents say it strips out the essential parliamentary-control element kept in a near-identical rival text.
- **The backdrop charge:** the mover claims Parliament has received no Fund report since 2018 and that the board is absent from the legally required UBO register.
- **The rub:** whether this is a genuine tightening of transparency over a near-100-million-euro public guarantee, or a watered-down copy that quietly trades real parliamentary control for after-the-fact notification.
deep_facts: Amendment no. 1, tabled by Olivier Willocx (MR), replaces article 3 of the ordinance so as to rewrite article 23 of the 1999 ordinance in full (CRI, 27 Jun 2025).

Under the amendment's text, the board (conseil d'administration) draws up the Fund's balance sheet and results account each 31 December and transmits them directly, with the board report and the report of the government-appointed auditor (reviseur), to the government and the Parliament, at the latest on 30 June of the following year (CRI, 27 Jun 2025).

The mover's stated grounds: the existing 30 April transmission deadline is materially impossible because accounts are systematically approved in May; and a committee-added article 19.1 created parallel reporting logic with article 23 without articulating or removing the old obligations, described as confused and redundant — hence a proposal to modernise article 23 as a single clear provision (CRI, 27 Jun 2025).

Difference from a near-identical earlier amendment (Team Fouad Ahidar, supported in committee by PTB and MR): the MR version asks for a notification to Parliament rather than an avis (opinion) of Parliament before adding a credit tranche; opponents characterise this as removing the essential parliamentary-control element (CRI, 27 Jun 2025).

The mover's transparency charges: no annual report, balance sheet or results account has been transmitted to the assembly directly from the Guarantee Fund since 2018 (last report 2018; amount cited 61 million euros), contrary to article 23 of the 1999 ordinance; and the Fund's administrators are not found in the UBO register, a legal obligation; he also notes article 11 requires Parliament to designate three representatives to the Fund, which he says has not happened (CRI, 27 Jun 2025).

Opponents' reply: the requested information (encours des engagements, default rate, premiums received) already appears in the Fund's annual accounts; activity reports are on the finance&invest.brussels site (2023 report pages 38-39); the board already informs the competent minister past a 75% threshold under the arrete of 25 May 2022; and a Fund official answered all committee questions — so the amendment was judged redundant and without added value (CRI, 27 Jun 2025).

Procedural note: a near-identical Team Fouad Ahidar amendment was tabled to the same text; the dispute on this amendment turned substantially on the MR having supported that earlier amendment in committee days before, then tabling its own (CRI, 27 Jun 2025).
BXL-2425-00029-v5.deep_lectura:
**Analyst read** *(inference — not stated verbatim in the record)*

- The fight is only partly about reporting dates: the load-bearing change is avis -> notification, which converts a parliamentary veto over extra credit tranches into a courtesy heads-up, materially weakening control even as the wrapper is sold as 'modernising transparency'.
- Tabling a near-verbatim copy of a rival's amendment, minus the control element, lets the mover claim the transparency high ground while declining to hand the rival group a co-authorship win — the procedural theatre is the substance.
- The 'no report since 2018 / absent UBO entry / undesignated representatives' charges, if borne out, undercut the majority's core defence that existing controls make new ones redundant — the existing controls may simply not be operating.
- A 30 April-to-30 June deadline shift is defensible on accounting calendars, but bundling it with the notification downgrade means a member who agrees on dates cannot vote the fix without also accepting the weaker control.
BXL-2425-00029-v5.raw_fr: Un amendement n° 1, depose par M. Olivier Willocx, remplace l'article 3 afin de reecrire integralement l'article 23 de l'ordonnance de 1999 : le conseil d'administration arrete chaque 31 decembre le bilan et le compte de resultat du Fonds, transmis directement, avec le rapport du conseil d'administration et celui du reviseur, au gouvernement et au Parlement au plus tard le 30 juin de l'annee suivante. L'auteur invoque une mise en conformite et la modernisation d'un article juge confus et redondant.
